title: From Open Mic to Game Show: Inside JavaScript Jam Live's React Miami Takeover
outline: Introduction: the chaos and charm of live community spaces
Meet the hosts: JavaScript Jam Live and the Edgio team
The React Miami partnership and what it means for the community
Miami Jam: reinventing the speaker interview as a game show
Why audience participation is the heart of the format
Lessons in live event production and community building
draft:
Anyone who has ever hosted a live online event knows the truth: something will go wrong. The only question is when. The latest episode of JavaScript Jam Live, a Twitter Spaces-based open mic for all things JavaScript and web development, opened with exactly that kind of moment. The Space showed as started on the host's phone, yet nobody else could see or join it. The fix, as it turned out, was nothing more than patience. Wait a minute or two, and the platform quietly sorts itself out. It was a small hiccup, but it set the tone for an episode that was equal parts technical lesson, community celebration, and sneak preview of something genuinely new.

The hosts laughed it off with a reference to an old Demotivators poster of the Titanic: maybe your role is to be a lesson for others. That self-deprecating humor is part of what makes community-run spaces like this one work. Nobody pretends to be infallible. As host Scott Steinlage put it, it does not matter how much you know about tech; there is always something waiting to make you look like a fool. The important thing is that everything works eventually, and the show goes on.

For those unfamiliar, JavaScript Jam Live bills itself as an open mic for anything JavaScript and web development related, and it takes that mission seriously. Audience participation is not just tolerated; it is actively encouraged. Whether you are a beginner writing your first lines of code or a seasoned engineer with years of production experience, the hosts want to hear from you. Questions, comments, opinions, even disagreements are all welcome, because the best conversations in these spaces tend to come from the audience rather than the stage. That philosophy of openness runs through everything the show does.

The hosting crew for this episode included Ishan Anand, VP of Product at Edgio; Anthony Campolo, a developer advocate at Edgio; and Scott Steinlage, a technical community manager at the same company. They were joined by Dev Agrawal, a fellow media partner, and Michelle, one of the organizers of React Miami herself, who dropped in to hear what the crew had planned. Her presence was a nice vote of confidence: the conference organizers had essentially given the media partners a green light to do whatever they liked, and she was listening in, curious to see the results.

The big news was the collaboration between JavaScript Jam Live and React Miami, which Scott immediately rebranded as React Miami Month. Going forward, the show will feature more speakers from the React Miami lineup, talking about topics that align with their conference talks. Importantly, Scott was careful to reassure regular listeners that the traditional JavaScript Jam vibe would not change. The format, the open mic energy, the welcoming attitude toward speakers of all levels: all of that stays. The partnership simply adds more value on top, including some extra goodies the team teased for later.

The centerpiece of the collaboration, though, is something called Miami Jam, and it is a genuinely clever idea. Dev explained that he wanted to move away from the typical interview or panel format, where a few speakers come on and answer predictable questions about their topics and motivations. Instead, Miami Jam will be structured like a game show. Speakers will face trivia-style questions about React, weird quirks in JavaScript or TypeScript, or anything adjacent to the ecosystem. They might be asked to guess which library is being used in a code snippet, or to answer a question about another speaker's talk topic.

Here is where the format gets interesting. The trivia is not just for entertainment; it is a Trojan horse for substance. Each question becomes a natural segue into deeper conversation. When a speaker answers a question about their topic, the hosts can follow up on their motivation for giving the talk, their experience in the industry, and the work that brought them to React Miami in the first place. The game show structure lowers the stakes and raises the energy, making it easier for speakers to relax, share stories, and even interact with each other rather than just with the hosts. It is collaborative by design.

The audience is not left out of the fun, either. Attendees at the live show will get to engage with speakers beyond the usual Q&A. In a delightful twist, if an audience member asks a question, they may get to decide how many points the speaker earns for answering it. That kind of mechanic turns passive listeners into active participants and gives everyone in the room a stake in how the show unfolds. It is a small detail, but it reflects a bigger insight: people remember events they helped shape far more than events they merely watched.

There are a few broader takeaways here for anyone involved in developer relations, community building, or event production. First, technical difficulties are not failures; they are opportunities to model grace under pressure. The hosts turned a platform glitch into a teaching moment for other Twitter Spaces hosts within the first minute of the show. Second, partnerships between community shows and conferences can be more than logo swaps. By giving media partners creative freedom, React Miami is getting content that feels authentic rather than promotional. Third, format innovation matters. The panel interview is comfortable, but comfort can breed predictability. A game show format creates surprise, laughter, and memorable moments while still delivering the insight audiences came for.

As web development communities continue to gather in hybrid spaces, part online, part in person, experiments like Miami Jam point the way forward. They respect the audience's time, they honor the speakers' expertise, and they never take themselves too seriously. If this episode of JavaScript Jam Live is any indication, React Miami Month is going to be a great time, whether you are on stage answering trivia or in the audience deciding how many points the answer was worth. Keep an eye out for upcoming episodes featuring React Miami speakers, and if you have a question or an opinion, do not be shy. Request the mic. That is what the open mic is for.
